idiom_name: builtin filter(predicate, iterable) / generator-expression if-clause (fnmatch.filter for pattern criteria)
implementation_notes: The operation is built in and lazy: `filter(pred, msgs)` and the generator expression `(m for m in msgs if pred(m))` are the canonical realizations, so there is no filter object to design; for pattern-shaped criteria (routing keys, topic names, filenames) the standard library even names the pattern - `fnmatch.filter(names, pat)` and `fnmatch.filterfalse(names, pat)`. A class-based MessageFilter is warranted only when the criterion must be selected from configuration, carry state (counters, dedup cache) or be a named, injectable component - and then a small callable object or functools.partial is enough.
code_sketch:
def interesting(msg: dict) -> bool:
    return msg["headers"].get("item_type") == "widget"

for msg in consumer:                    # one predicate call per message
    if not interesting(msg):
        dropped += 1                    # or dead_letter.send(msg)
        continue
    handle(msg)

# lazy alternative: accepted = filter(interesting, consumer)
pitfalls: filter() returns an iterator: it is single-use, and because it is lazy an exception raised by the predicate surfaces at consumption time, far from where the filter was built.

fnmatch (used by fnmatch.filter) normalises case through os.path.normcase on case-insensitive platforms; routing keys and topic names are case-sensitive, so build the predicate from fnmatchcase instead.
Mutating the dict or object the predicate inspects while iterating the same collection raises RuntimeError (dictionary changed size during iteration) - filter a copy or collect first.
